q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with one equivalent of HBr at 40 °C, conditions under which the products equilibrate. Which compound is the major product?
h: Protonation at C1 gives an allylic cation with positive charge shared by C2 and C4. Which of the two possible bromides has the more substituted (more stable) alkene?
w: Protonation of C1 gives a resonance-stabilized allylic cation (charge on C2 and C4). Bromide can add at C2 (1,2-addition, 3-bromo-1-butene) or at C4 (1,4-addition, 1-bromo-2-butene). At 40 °C the products interconvert, so the more stable one wins: A, (E)-1-bromo-2-butene, whose internal disubstituted alkene is more stable than the monosubstituted alkene of the 1,2-product.
x: This is the 1,2-product: it forms faster and dominates at low temperature (kinetic control), but it is less stable.
C would require protonation at C2 to give a primary, non-allylic cation; protonation at C1 gives the allylic cation instead.
D, a vinyl bromide, would need bromide to add to a vinyl cation; the allylic cation never puts charge there.

q: A mixture rich in 3-bromo-1-butene, made from 1,3-butadiene and HBr at −80 °C, is warmed to 40 °C and becomes mostly 1-bromo-2-butene. What is the best explanation?
c: At 40 °C the allylic C–Br bond ionizes reversibly, so the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product
At 40 °C the activation energy for forming 1-bromo-2-butene becomes lower than that for 3-bromo-1-butene
3-Bromo-1-butene becomes the less stable isomer only at higher temperatures
Bromide ion is a stronger nucleophile at higher temperature and attacks only the terminal carbon
h: Both products share the same allylic cation. What does added heat allow the kinetic product to do?
w: At −80 °C the products form irreversibly, so the faster-forming 1,2-product dominates (kinetic control). On warming, the allylic C–Br bond can ionize back to the same allylic cation and bromide; repeated ionization and recombination let the system reach equilibrium, which favors the more stable 1,4-product with its more substituted alkene. Reversible ionization leads to thermodynamic control.
x: Temperature changes how many molecules can cross each barrier, not which barrier is lower; the 1,2-pathway still has the lower TS.
Relative stability does not flip on warming: 1-bromo-2-butene is the more stable isomer at both temperatures.
Product ratios under equilibrium control are set by stabilities, not by nucleophile strength; bromide attacks both cation termini.

q: Use the bond dissociation energies in the table to estimate ΔH° for CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl.
h: ΔH° = (energy of bonds broken) − (energy of bonds formed).
w: Bonds broken: CH3–H (439) + Cl–Cl (242) = 681 kJ/mol. Bonds formed: CH3–Cl (350) + H–Cl (431) = 781 kJ/mol. ΔH° = 681 − 781 = −100 kJ/mol.
x: This is formed − broken; breaking bonds costs energy, so ΔH° = broken − formed.
+8 kJ/mol is only the first propagation step (CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl• → CH<sub>3</sub>• + HCl), not the overall reaction.
−108 kJ/mol is only the second propagation step (CH<sub>3</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl•).

q: Use the table to estimate ΔH° for the step CH<sub>4</sub> + Br• → CH<sub>3</sub>• + HBr. What does the Hammond postulate then say about its transition state?
c: +73 kJ/mol; the transition state is late and resembles CH<sub>3</sub>• + HBr
+73 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
−73 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
−101 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
h: Only one bond breaks and one forms in this step. Then: does an uphill step have a reactant-like or product-like TS?
w: Broken: CH3–H, 439 kJ/mol. Formed: H–Br, 366 kJ/mol. ΔH° = 439 − 366 = +73 kJ/mol, an endothermic step. The Hammond postulate places the TS of an endothermic step close to its higher-energy products, so the TS is late and resembles CH3• + HBr, with the C–H bond nearly broken.
x: The ΔH° is right, but an endothermic step has a late, product-like TS, not an early one.
The sign is reversed: breaking a 439 kJ/mol bond and forming a 366 kJ/mol bond costs energy.
−101 kJ/mol is the other propagation step (CH<sub>3</sub>• + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Br + Br•), not this one.

q: Which labeled C–H bond in 4-methyl-1-pentene has the lowest bond dissociation energy?
h: The weakest C–H bond is the one whose homolysis gives the most stable radical.
w: Breaking a C–H at c gives an allylic radical, delocalized over two carbons by resonance with the C=C, so this bond is the weakest (about 350 kJ/mol). Homolysis at d gives an ordinary 3° radical (about 400 kJ/mol), and vinylic C–H bonds at a and b are the strongest (about 460 kJ/mol) because the sp2 vinyl radical is unstable. The C–H bond at c.
x: A 3° radical is stabilized by hyperconjugation, but less than the resonance-delocalized allylic radical from c.
This is a vinylic C–H; vinyl radicals are very unstable, so this bond is among the strongest.
This is a vinylic C–H on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon; its homolysis gives an unstable vinyl radical.

q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction by 11.4 kJ/mol without changing the pre-exponential factor. At 25 °C (298 K), the rate constant increases by a factor of about
h: From k = A e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, the ratio k<sub>new</sub>/k<sub>old</sub> = e<sup>ΔEa/RT</sup>.
w: knew/kold = e11 400/(8.314 × 298) = e4.60 ≈ 100. At room temperature every 5.7 kJ/mol of barrier is worth a factor of 10 in rate.
x: A factor of 10 corresponds to only 5.7 kJ/mol; 11.4 kJ/mol is twice that, so the factor is 10<sup>2</sup>.
4.6 is the exponent (ΔEa/RT), not the ratio; the ratio is e<sup>4.6</sup>.
A factor of 1000 would need about 17 kJ/mol of barrier lowering.

q: A reaction A → B + C has ΔH° = +20 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +80 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>. Which describes ΔG° and K<sub>eq</sub> at 25 °C (298 K)?
h: Convert ΔS° to kJ before using ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; then recall the sign link between ΔG° and K.
w: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 20 − (298)(0.080) = 20 − 23.8 = −3.8 kJ/mol. A negative ΔG° means Keq > 1 (here e3800/2478 ≈ 4.6). ΔG° = −3.8 kJ/mol and Keq > 1: the entropy gain from making two molecules outweighs the endothermic bond breaking at this temperature.
x: The sign is flipped; −TΔS° (−23.8) outweighs +20, so ΔG° is negative.
This adds TΔS° instead of subtracting it; ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
ΔG° is right, but a negative ΔG° gives K > 1, since ΔG° = −RT ln K.

q: Which reaction has ΔS° > 0?
h: Count molecules on each side; making more independent molecules raises entropy.
w: Dehydration turns one molecule into two, increasing the number of ways energy and matter can be distributed: ΔS° > 0 for the dehydration. The other three combine two molecules into one, so ΔS° < 0. This is why eliminations are favored at high temperature.
x: Hydrogenation joins two molecules into one, so entropy decreases.
The Diels–Alder reaction joins two molecules into one ring, so entropy decreases.
HBr addition joins two molecules into one, so entropy decreases.

q: Which reaction is best described by this energy diagram?
h: How many transition states are there, and is there any intermediate?
w: The diagram has one transition state and no intermediate: a single concerted step. The SN2 reaction of a primary bromide with cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent breaks C–Br as C–CN forms in one step. CH3CH2Br + NaCN in DMSO.
x: Solvolysis of a 3° bromide is S<sub>N</sub>1, with a carbocation intermediate, so its diagram has at least two transition states.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration (E1) has several steps (protonation, loss of water, deprotonation) and two intermediates.
HBr addition goes through a carbocation intermediate, so its diagram shows two transition states.

q: This diagram represents the acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-propanol by the E1 mechanism. Which point corresponds to the tert-butyl cation?
h: List the steps in order: protonation of OH, loss of water, loss of H<sup>+</sup>. Which valleys are intermediates, and which comes second?
w: E1 dehydration has three steps. Step 1 (TS A) protonates the OH to give the oxonium ion, intermediate B. Step 2 (TS C, the highest point, rate-determining) loses water to give the carbocation, intermediate D. Step 3 (TS E) removes a β-hydrogen to give the alkene. The carbocation is higher in energy than the oxonium ion, as the diagram shows.
x: B is the first intermediate, the protonated alcohol (alkyloxonium ion), formed before water leaves.
C is a transition state (a maximum), the point where the C–O bond is partly broken; the cation is the valley after it.
E is the transition state for removing a proton from the carbocation, not an intermediate.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ionizes in water far faster than 2-bromopropane. Which explanation is best?
c: Ionization is endothermic, so its transition state resembles the carbocation, and the more stable 3° cation lowers it more
The 3° bromide has a stronger C–Br bond, so its transition state is reached earlier along the path
The ionization step is exothermic, so its transition state resembles the alkyl bromide, which is more stable for the 3° compound
Water attacks the 3° carbon more easily because it is less hindered
h: Use the Hammond postulate: an uphill step has a transition state that looks like its product.
w: Ionization of an alkyl bromide to a carbocation is strongly endothermic, so the TS is late and has much carbocation character. Whatever stabilizes the carbocation (here, three alkyl groups giving more hyperconjugation in the 3° cation) also stabilizes the TS and lowers Ea. The more stable 3° cation lowers the TS.
x: A stronger bond would slow ionization; the rate difference comes from carbocation stability, not bond strength.
Ionization is endothermic, not exothermic; and a more stable reactant would raise, not lower, the barrier.
A 3° carbon is more hindered, not less; and water does not attack in the rate-determining step of S<sub>N</sub>1.

q: Which two labeled carbons of 3-buten-2-one are electrophilic sites, where a nucleophile can add?
h: Draw the resonance form that moves the C=C π electrons toward the oxygen. Which carbons carry the + charge?
w: The carbonyl carbon c is δ+ (C=O ↔ C+–O−). Because the C=C is conjugated with C=O, a second resonance form moves the C=C π electrons toward the carbonyl and places the + charge on the terminal β carbon a. Carbons a and c are electrophilic (1,2- and 1,4-addition sites).
x: Carbon b (the α carbon) never carries + charge in any resonance form; the charge alternates to a.
b is not electrophilic, and the conjugate (β) site a pairs with the carbonyl carbon c.
The methyl carbon d is not electrophilic; it is not part of the conjugated system.

q: Diethyl ether and BF<sub>3</sub> combine as shown. Which statement describes the roles of the reactants?
c: The ether oxygen is the nucleophile (Lewis base); boron is the electrophile (Lewis acid)
Boron is the nucleophile (Lewis base); the ether oxygen is the electrophile (Lewis acid)
A fluorine of BF<sub>3</sub> is the nucleophile; the ether oxygen is the electrophile
The ether oxygen is the electrophile because it ends up with a positive formal charge
h: Which atom has a lone pair to donate, and which has an empty orbital?
w: Boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital, so it accepts an electron pair: electrophile (Lewis acid). The ether oxygen donates a lone pair: nucleophile (Lewis base). O is the nucleophile, B is the electrophile. The formal charges in the adduct (O+, B−) result from that electron donation.
x: The roles are reversed: boron has an empty orbital and no lone pair to donate.
Fluorine's lone pairs are held tightly and the new bond in the product is O–B, not F–O.
The + formal charge on oxygen in the product is the result of donating its lone pair; that is what a nucleophile does.

q: Which carbocation is the least stable?
h: Where is the empty orbital in each cation, and can it overlap with a π system?
w: In the phenyl cation A the positive charge sits in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, at right angles to the aromatic π system, so there is no resonance stabilization, and the high s character of the empty orbital makes it very unstable. The benzyl and allyl cations are stabilized by resonance, and the cyclohexyl cation is an ordinary 2° cation.
x: The allyl cation is resonance stabilized: its empty p orbital overlaps with the C=C π bond.
The benzyl cation is strongly resonance stabilized by the ring, unlike the phenyl cation.
The cyclohexyl cation is an ordinary secondary cation with hyperconjugation; it is far more stable than an aryl cation.

q: 3-Methyl-1-butene reacts with HCl to give two alkyl chlorides. Which product comes from a carbocation that underwent a 1,2-hydride shift?
h: Protonate the alkene to give the more substituted cation first. Is there a neighboring hydrogen whose shift gives a more stable cation?
w: Markovnikov protonation at C1 gives the 2° cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 gives the 3° cation at C3, and chloride capture there gives A, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Capture before the shift gives B, the other product of the reaction.
x: This is the unrearranged Markovnikov product, formed when chloride traps the 2° cation before any shift.
This is the anti-Markovnikov product; it would need a primary cation, which HCl addition does not form.
This is a primary chloride (1-chloro-2-methylbutane); it would need a primary cation, which neither protonation nor a hydride shift produces here.

q: Which carbocation is expected to rearrange by a 1,2-shift to a more stable carbocation?
h: For each cation, ask what a 1,2-hydride or methyl shift would produce, and whether the new cation is more substituted.
w: In A, a 1,2-methyl shift from the neighboring quaternary carbon turns the 2° cation into a 3° cation, so it rearranges. B is already 3°. In C (2-butyl cation), a hydride shift from C3 gives another 2-butyl cation, no gain. In D (cyclohexyl), any hydride shift gives another 2° cyclohexyl cation.
x: This is already a 3° cation; any 1,2-shift would give a less stable 2° or 1° cation.
A hydride shift in the 2-butyl cation gives an identical 2° cation, so there is no driving force.
Every carbon next to the cyclohexyl cation is a CH<sub>2</sub>; a hydride shift gives another 2° cation of the same kind.

q: An alkyl bromide (RBr) reacts with sodium azide. Based on the initial-rate data, what is the rate law?
h: Compare pairs of experiments in which only one concentration changes.
w: Experiments 1 → 2: doubling [RBr] (azide fixed) doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in RBr. Experiments 1 → 3: tripling [N3−] (RBr fixed) leaves the rate unchanged, so it is zero order in azide. rate = k[RBr], the rate law expected for an SN1 reaction whose slow step is ionization.
x: Tripling [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] did not change the rate, so azide does not appear in the rate law.
The rate depends on [RBr] (experiments 1 and 2) and not on [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>].
Doubling [RBr] doubled the rate; second order would have quadrupled it.

q: Two irreversible pathways from the same intermediate give products X and Y. The transition state leading to X is 4.0 kJ/mol lower than the one leading to Y. At 25 °C (298 K), what is the approximate X : Y ratio?
h: Under kinetic control, [X]/[Y] = k<sub>X</sub>/k<sub>Y</sub> = e<sup>ΔΔG‡/RT</sup>.
x: This uses 10<sup>1.61</sup> ≈ 41 instead of e<sup>1.61</sup>; rate ratios from ΔΔG<sup>‡</sup> use the natural exponential.
This comes from dividing 4.0 (kJ) by RT in J, giving e<sup>0.0016</sup> ≈ 1; convert to 4000 J/mol first.
The ratio is reversed: the pathway with the lower transition state is faster, so X is the major product.

q: An intermediate can form product A or product B. The table gives energies relative to the intermediate. Which statement is correct?
c: A dominates at low temperature (kinetic product); B dominates when the system can equilibrate (thermodynamic product)
B dominates at low temperature (kinetic product); A dominates when the system can equilibrate (thermodynamic product)
A dominates under all conditions because its transition state is lower
B dominates under all conditions because it is the more stable product
h: Kinetic control compares transition-state energies; thermodynamic control compares product energies.
w: A has the lower transition state (60 vs 70 kJ/mol), so it forms faster and dominates when products cannot revert (low temperature, short times). B is lower in energy (−25 vs −10 kJ/mol), so it dominates once the reactions are reversible and equilibrium is reached. A is the kinetic product; B is the thermodynamic product.
x: This swaps the definitions: the lower transition state (A) makes A the kinetic product.
When the reactions become reversible, the more stable product B accumulates, so A does not win under all conditions.
Under irreversible, low-temperature conditions the faster-forming A wins, so B does not dominate under all conditions.

q: A mixture of methane and oxygen can sit unchanged at 25 °C for years even though combustion has a very negative ΔG°. What is the reason?
c: The activation energy is very high, so the rate at 25 °C is extremely small
K<sub>eq</sub> for combustion is less than 1 at 25 °C
ΔS° for combustion is negative, which makes the reaction non-spontaneous
Exothermic reactions do not start unless their ΔH° is positive
h: Thermodynamics says whether a reaction is favorable; kinetics says how fast it goes.
w: A very negative ΔG° means Keq is huge, so combustion is favorable. But the rate depends on the activation energy, and breaking the strong C–H and O=O bonds requires a large Ea. The barrier is high, so the reaction is extremely slow at 25 °C until a spark supplies energy.
x: A very negative ΔG° means K<sub>eq</sub> is much greater than 1.
ΔG° already includes the entropy term; a very negative ΔG° means spontaneous whatever the sign of ΔS°.
This is not a rule; reaction rates depend on E<sub>a</sub>, not on the sign of ΔH°.
